accuracy.evidence: The curriculum wording matches the published documents: the English national curriculum (DfE 2013) Years 5 and 6 writing composition statements 'identifying the audience for and purpose of the writing, selecting the appropriate form' and 'selecting appropriate grammar and vocabulary, understanding how such choices can change and enhance meaning', and the formal/informal statement; Common Core W.4.4, W.5.4 (task, purpose and audience) and L.4.3c, L.5.3 (formal vs informal contexts). Every task has a defensible single purpose and form; the five tone versions of the hall message move monotonically from slang to a formal letter with Yours faithfully after Dear Sir or Madam; the simplified sentences keep the original facts. p2, p3, m6 and m9 give whole answers at every parameter value.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented KS2 composition errors: topic given for purpose (m8 and the purpose step feedback), defaulting to one form (form step and Challenge distractors), chatty openings to officials (tone dial too-chatty feedback, Challenge Hiya option), over-formality to friends (dial too-stiff feedback, 'formal is always best' item), simplifying by losing content (lol distractors), and mixing forms inside one piece (Once upon a time and Step 1 lines in the letter).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagaud is a planning lab: it classifies tasks by the four purposes, drags task cards onto drawn page outlines of five text types, uses a continuous tone dial that rewrites one message at five formality levels for three readers, swaps hard words for a younger audience with a readability bar, and finds tone and form slips in a whole letter. Formal and informal English (185, flagreg) only spots and swaps informal words; this lab's purpose, form, dial and younger-reader steps have no counterpart there, and the lab_distinct gate passes.

lab_teaches.evidence: The steps follow the planning order writers use: purpose, then form, then tone, then vocabulary, then a check of a finished piece. Wrong choices give the definition of what was picked and why the task needs something else (for example 'A review gives an opinion, reasons and a rating. This task needs a letter.').

predictions.evidence: Two predictions: the form for asking the head for a bike rack (tempting: a story, because the topic is fun) and where the dial belongs for the town council (tempting: it does not matter). Both are revealed against what the child does next.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six Challenge questions spanning purpose, form, openings, younger readers, reviews and the 'formal is always best' belief, with a specific hint for each of the twelve wrong options, a streak counter and Another question.

readability.evidence: Kid text explains audience, purpose, form and tone with one concrete example each, at a Year 5 reading level, four paragraphs. Adult text keeps sentences short (passes the FK grade 10 check) and defines purpose, form, text type, tone and register.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph carries a definition, a worked example or a named mistake; the family tip gives one concrete activity with the exact three formats to try.

mobile.evidence: Tall 1.25 canvas on phones, purpose chips and form tiles sized for thumbs, the tone dial has More chatty, More formal and Send buttons as well as the drag, every canvas tap has a button twin, and the iPhone 13 walk passes every step.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas aria-label follows each message, buttons carry descriptive labels (Purpose: persuade, Line 4: …), feedback is in a live region, text is drawn in the theme text colour over pale fills, and axe passes in light and dark themes.
